newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wins re-election, Republicans hold Senate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wins re-election, Republicans hold Senate.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Democrat Bill Clinton won re-election as U.S. president on Tuesday, routing Republican Bob Dole on the back of a healthy economy, but Republicans held their majority in the Senate.
Computerized voter tallies by television networks projected Clinton the winner in 26 of the 50 U.S. states to 12 for Dole by 10 p.m. EST (0300 GMT Wednesday).
That gave Clinton 281 Electoral College votes to 119 for Dole, 21 more than the 270 needed to win under the indirect U.S. system.

Clinton, 50, the first president from the post-war "baby boom" generation, also became the first Democrat re-elected to the presidency in more than half a century -- since Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1944.

Dole spokesman Nelson Warfield conceded defeat, saying "Bob Dole has completed his last political mission with courage and honour. Even in defeat, he has much to claim in the way of success...(leading) his party in this election, representing trust and conservative principles."
The Dole campaign later withdrew the statement, saying it had been issued in error and they had not conceded.
Despite his sweep of key states, the victory fell short of the landslide for Clinton that most public opinion polls had predicted.
With more than a third of the vote counted, Clinton had scored 50 percent of the popular vote, to Dole's 42 percent and Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's eight percent.
The president had gone all out for an absolute majority that would have enabled him to claim a wider mandate for his second term.
Republicans held their majority in the Senate and seemed well placed to keep the House of Representatives as well, two years after seizing control of both houses for the first time in 40 years.
If that trend was confirmed by late results on the west coast, it would be the first time Republicans managed to hold Congress for two consecutive elections since 1928.

Democrats and their labour union allies spent tens of millions of dollars in an effort to recapture control of Congress. Their failure would force the two parties to work with one another and put a check on both.
But for Clinton any victory at all was sweet vindication, befitting the political legend of a man who once dubbed himself "The Comeback Kid."

Exactly two years ago he was written off as a one-term lame duck by many analysts after disgruntled voters tossed his Democrats out of Congress in droves and handed control of both houses to the Republicans for the first time in 40 years.

The message from voters on Tuesday was very different from the discontent they felt then: the country is now on the right track, they told pollsters as they left ballot stations and their personal financial outlook is much rosier.
They did not seem much to care about Dole's insistent message that Clinton is not very honest or trustworthy.

Clinton did particularly well among women and senior citizens. He had focused heavily on the issues of education and preserving government programmes for the old and sick in his campaign, attacking Republicans as uncaring and obsessed with dismantling big government.

For Dole, 73, a former Senate majority leader from Kansas who was badly wounded as an infantryman in World War II, it was the end of long, distinguished career in public service and of his dream of winning "one last mission" at the pinnacle of power.
Opinion polls had indicated with brutal regularity for months that his hope was Quixotic, that Americans were not prepared to turn back the clock and put one of his elder generation in command.
In the end, Dole's hope of becoming another Harry Truman, the upset champion of American politicians, turned out to be just a grand dream.
Perot was again in the race as a third-force candidate, for the Reform Party, but he appeared to be much less of a factor than in 1992 when he won 19 percent of the vote.
Final results would depend on voting far into the night on the U.S. west coast, but the dimensions of Clinton's victory were apparent early on.

He swept Dole in most of the big prize electoral-vote states, taking away usually Republican Florida and Ohio among others and adding the big industrial states of New York, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Illinois and New Jersey.
Dole could retaliate only in Texas and North Carolina from the major states plus a handful of smaller ones.

Among the early congressional results, arch-conservative Republican Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, was re-elected in North Carolina, as was 93-year-old Republican Strom Thurmond in South Carolina.
Clinton's home state of Arkansas bucked its native son at the Senate level, electing newcomer Tim Hutchinson as the first Republican senator in over 100 years.
The tale of Clinton's victory seemed clearly to be of voters rating personal security and national prosperity far above the character issues and tax-cut promises Dole pushed.
ABC News reported 58 percent of those leaving the polls rated the economy in good shape.
That compared with only 19 percent four years ago, when Clinton ousted Republican George Bush by hammering at discontent with a weak economy.

NBC said its exit poll also showed 58 percent believed the country was headed in the right direction, compared to two years ago when 60 percent thought it was on the wrong track and Republicans won Congress.
